title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority delays vessel, truck and train movements and pushes scheduling onto manual processes at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The Santos Port Authority (APS), which runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its internal IT systems on 6 November and confirmed a cyberattack on 10 November. Identification, access-control and digital port-operations tools went down, delaying vessel, truck and train movements, and route scheduling, vessel arrival records and billing were handled by hand. By 16 November the main systems were in final tests and about 70% of affected file backups had been recovered; vessel movements and port access continued throughout. CNN Brasil reports the malware was already on the network and activated after a 6 November power cut. The attacker and entry route are undisclosed, and the Federal Police are investigating. For railways serving ports, an authority’s IT outage reaches train scheduling and gate access, so the interchange needs a tested manual fallback (editorial assessment).

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: The Rio Times (16 Nov 2026, citing the Santos Port Authority); FreshPlaza (11 Nov 2026, vessel, truck and train delays; access-control impact); CyberDelegate (17 Nov 2026, citing Folha de S.Paulo, CNN Brasil and Agência Brasil; ~70% of backups recovered); rail relevance is our editorial assessment

items.title: France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s refrigeration sabotage as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks
items.content_text: France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against the people behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned on 16 November that settings were also changed at French blood-service sites. US and Israeli officials have told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers also sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. No rail target is reported, but the same weak point, an internet-reachable controller with a default password, exists in station and depot building systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. Belgium’s interior minister said on 12 November that evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution (see the Iran sabotage card above); a pro-Russian claim is unverified. Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today.

items.title: Coast Guard cyber teams board tankers as US officials eye Iran in up to 50 attacks on energy shipping that feeds rail-served terminals
items.content_text: US officials told the Wall Street Journal, in a report carried on 23–24 November, that Iran is the main suspect in as many as 50 cyberattacks on tankers carrying oil, liquefied gas and chemicals. The Coast Guard sent cyber teams to at least four vessels nearing US shores, including the Texas-bound VL Prosperity and Kohaku; the VL Prosperity’s captain received a ransom note. Some officials also name Russia, one official called four of the attacks a minor nuisance, and no ship is reported disabled. No rail system is involved, but it is the third transport-linked campaign this autumn after the Santos port attack and DHS’s warning on Iranian targeting of transportation. Railways that load or unload at energy and chemical terminals share those terminals’ networks and edge devices (editorial assessment).

items.title: Maersk confirms hackers stole data from a legacy logistics system it inherited through an acquisition, as a ransomware group demands $5 million
items.content_text: Maersk confirmed on 11 November that a threat actor breached a system belonging to LF Logistics, the Asian contract-logistics company it bought from Li & Fung in 2022, and took data. The WhiteArmor ransomware group listed Maersk on its leak site on 7 November, claims about 100 GB, including driver records with plaintext passwords and super-administrator accounts, and demands $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. Maersk says the incident is isolated to a local system, its evidence so far indicates no sensitive data was disclosed, there is no sign of impact on other systems or on customer API and EDI connections, and it does not expect operational disruption. It has not said when or how the intrusion happened. For freight and intermodal operators, systems inherited through acquisitions or run by partners are a common blind spot (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these gateways often guard remote access into rail control centres, and ESXi often hosts SCADA, passenger-information and crew systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: Norway says the Equinor and Skagerak intrusions came through Microsoft’s Azure API Management, a cloud service many operators use to share operational data
items.content_text: On 23 November Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said an unidentified actor has been stealing access tokens and other sensitive data from Microsoft Azure API Management (APIM), and that energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi were among those hit. Equinor detected its intrusion on 17 November and contained it by 20 November; both firms say production carried on normally, and NSM found no service disruption. A reported, non-public Microsoft notice says an issue in older “Classic” APIM tiers was closed on 19 November; Microsoft has issued credential-rotation guidance but has not publicly linked it to Norway. No rail operator is named. Rail and transit operators that publish train-running, passenger-information or maintenance data through cloud APIs should treat those keys as exposed (editorial assessment).

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For rail and transit, transportation is now named in the official US threat picture (editorial assessment).

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total; transport and logistics, the third-largest group, is where rail and intermodal operators sit. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October.

items.title: Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train”: Lumen exposes the throwaway relay chains the China-linked group uses to exploit SD-WAN and IT-management platforms — and lists rail among the sectors targeted
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs said on 28 October that the China-linked group Volt Typhoon has used a framework it calls “Silent Train” since November 2023 to reach targets without exposing its own infrastructure. Each operation runs through a fresh chain of typically four to six hops — rented servers abroad, then compromised small-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise appliances — assembled in under two minutes and cleaned up afterwards. The chains are aimed at management and control-plane platforms: Lumen ties the group to exploitation of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN CVE-2026-20127, VeloCloud Orchestrator CVE-2026-16812, N-able N-central CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, Versa Director and, with moderate confidence, a Quest KACE zero-day. Lumen names rail among the critical-infrastructure sectors targeted. No victim is named and no OT access is described; the N-central flaws matter again as new N-central chains are exploited (see Critical Advisories).

items.title: Claroty finds 65,000 game consoles, smart speakers and cars on critical-infrastructure networks, most of them on production segments
items.content_text: Claroty said on 17 November that, across 45 million devices at more than 30,000 critical-infrastructure sites, it found about 65,000 consumer gadgets that do not belong on operational networks: game consoles, smart-home and entertainment devices, and connected cars. Industrial sites held 963 game consoles, nearly 90% of them on production rather than guest networks. Thousands of Teslas, Fords and other vehicles were connected to site networks, almost none isolated on a guest segment, and Claroty cites six critical flaws in the Tesla Model 3 alone. The report does not break out rail. Depots, stations and control centres with staff Wi-Fi and vehicle chargers are exactly where such devices land on networks that also carry building, SCADA or maintenance traffic (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Rail control centres often run SCADA servers, passenger-information and crew systems as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to control-centre systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named. Where railways run these grid-control and RTU products for traction power, or RUGGEDCOM APE1808 in wayside networks, treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning (editorial assessment).

items.title: Siemens says the KEV-listed Node2Shell flaw reaches WinCC, WinCC OA and TIA Administrator, most with no fix yet, and flags an unfixable NTLM weakness in WinCC and PCS 7
items.content_text: Siemens has confirmed that Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS 9.8), the Brotli decoder flaw CISA added to KEV on 27 October, affects a long list of its industrial software; CISA republished the advisory as ICSA-26-321-03 on 17 November. Fixes exist for SIMATIC WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1), Braumat and Sistar. WinCC V7/V8, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC Unified PC Runtime, WinCC OA V3.21, TIA Administrator and User Management Component have no fix yet, and Siemens advises disabling Brotli compression where it is not needed. A second advisory (ICSA-26-321-08) covers CVE-2026-58114: WinCC, PCS 7 V9.1 and Process Historian still accept deprecated NTLM authentication, so an on-path attacker can relay a user’s login; several products will get no fix. Neither flaw is reported exploited against Siemens products. WinCC and WinCC OA run in some station, tunnel and traction-power SCADA (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November, which it calls a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, missing authorization checks, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and it removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Remote control and Intune integration stay blocked for now. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud, forcing it to take the management portal and APIs offline; it says mail flow continued, it has found no access to customer data, and the breach is unrelated to N-central. Many integrators manage control-centre and depot Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment).

items.title: Cisco ASA and FTD: an exploited zero-day lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the remote-access VPN firewall — in KEV, the 1 November federal deadline now passed, and no workaround
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 on 28 October for CVE-2026-76418 in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October. Where SSL VPN is enabled and a tunnel group — DefaultWEBVPNGroup included — is configured with secondary authentication, a crafted request from a remote, unauthenticated attacker makes the device reload; Cisco notes that a successful VPN login is not needed to reach the vulnerable code. Cisco scores it CVSS v3.1 8.6. It is a denial of service, not code execution, but each reload drops every VPN session and whatever else the firewall carries until it restarts. There are no workarounds: Cisco’s mitigation is to disable the tunnel-group list or remove secondary authentication, which it says weakens the VPN’s security. Fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48 and 9.24.1.27 or 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1. CISA added it to KEV on 29 October with a 1 November federal deadline, which has passed. Cisco has not named the attackers or described targets, and no rail or transit victim has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ASA and FTD are common at railway IT/OT boundaries and as the VPN that remote engineers and suppliers use, secondary authentication is exactly the stronger login operators add for that access, and older ASA and FTD flaws are among the entry routes in the SafePay advisory on this page.

items.title: The Linux kernel flaw used to root PAN-OS firewalls, CVE-2026-46300, is in KEV — and Siemens lists it in the Linux subsystem of S7-1500 MFP controllers, fixed in V3.1.7 but not for V3.1.5
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel flaw that Infosecurity Magazine and Cybersecurity Dive call “Fragnesia”, to KEV on 28 October with a 31 October federal deadline, now passed. When the kernel coalesces network-buffer fragments it can drop a marker that says they are shared, so ESP decryption runs in place over page-cache data and a low-privileged local user can write to the cached contents of files they should only be able to read, potentially gaining root. Red Hat scores it CVSS v3.1 7.8, and it is fixed upstream in 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33 and 7.0.10. CISA’s KEV entry says it can be chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to plant PHP web shells and run commands as root, and The Record and Infosecurity identify it as the kernel step in the PAN-OS compromises described in the PHP2Shell card above. On its own it is a local flaw: it does not let anyone in from the network, but it turns any foothold into root. The OT bridge is Siemens. Its advisories SSA-019113 and SSA-082556 cover the additional GNU/Linux subsystem of the SIMATIC S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP: Siemens lists CVE-2026-46300 for V3.1.6, fixed by updating to V3.1.7 or later, while V3.1.5 has no fix and is no longer maintained, leaving Siemens’ mitigations of running only trusted applications and restricting access to the Linux subsystem’s shell. No exploitation of a Siemens product has been reported. Keep it separate from CVE-2026-43284, a similar kernel flaw with public exploit code listed in Hitachi Energy’s CoreTec advisory, which is not in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: S7-1500 controllers run depot, workshop, tunnel-ventilation and station plant, and many trackside, telemetry and on-board gateways run embedded Linux, where a flaw like this turns a low-privileged foothold into full control of the device.

items.title: Moxa fixes a man-in-the-middle flaw in its Remote Connect client — but its OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway is end-of-life, with static keys and an SMS command-injection flaw that will not be fixed
items.content_text: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October for three flaws. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, Moxa) affects the MRC Client of Moxa Remote Connect Suite, versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0: because the client does not properly validate certificates when it takes an OpenVPN configuration supplied by the server, an attacker positioned between client and server could impersonate the server and read or alter the connection. Version 4.2.2 is not affected and, according to CERT-FR, the fix is obtained through Moxa technical support. The other two affect the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway: CVE-2026-111460 (v4.0 7.7), private keys for HTTPS and the device certificate authority embedded statically in the firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (v4.0 7.5), an operating-system command injection that an attacker with the required privileges can reach when SMS management is enabled. The gateway is end-of-life and no fix will be issued; Moxa’s mitigations are to reset the device so it regenerates its keys and to keep SMS management disabled, which is the default. No exploitation has been reported, and none of the three is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Moxa networking and cellular equipment is common across railways — on rolling stock, at stations and in wayside and telemetry cabinets — and remote-access clients like MRC are how engineers reach those sites from outside.

items.title: Bluetooth flaws let a nearby attacker apply or release trailer brakes on Elecbrakes controllers used by towing fleets, and the oldest model is still unpatched
items.content_text: Element Digital researchers found three Bluetooth flaws in Elecbrakes trailer brake controllers (EB2, VM1 and ELBC 2000), two rated critical, covering missing authentication and weak replay protection. An attacker within about 100 metres could engage or release a trailer’s brakes, or change braking force, without the driver doing anything. CISA published advisory ICSA-26-323-02 last week. Elecbrakes shipped firmware for EB2 and VM1 in early July and says about 60–70% of controllers in daily use have it; a fix for the older ELBC 2000 is still in progress. There is no evidence of malicious exploitation. Rail maintenance-of-way crews, signal and track contractors and road-rail vehicle fleets that tow equipment trailers should check whether they use these units (editorial assessment).

items.title: UK transport strategy asks operators to build cyber resilience into continuity plans, citing a £1.8bn cost for a week-long cyber outage of rail communications
items.content_text: The UK Department for Transport published its Transport Resilience Strategy on 2 November, with 22 commitments for the next five to ten years, including transport resilience standards, a Transport Resilience Network and a Transport Resilience Academy pilot. On cyber, it asks operators to make cyber resilience part of business-continuity planning by identifying vulnerabilities, mapping interdependencies and setting up response and recovery arrangements, aligned with the government’s National Cyber Action Plan. It cites KPMG research estimating that a reasonable-worst-case cyber incident on Network Rail’s train communications system, causing a week of disruption, could cost about £1.8bn: roughly £123.5m to Network Rail, £281.3m in passenger delay and £1.4bn in wider economic impact. In the scenario ETCS Level 2 services stop until systems are restored and other trains are slowed. KPMG rated the chance of systemic disruption within two years as low.
